title: The ghazals
hookLine: besides the Masnavi, Rumi left thousands of short love poems, many signed with Shams' name (Divan-e Shams)
last: WE WERE MADE FOR SOMETHING ELSE.

lines: A SONG SIGNED WITH A FRIEND'S NAME.
cards: A songwriter finishes a song, and where her own name should go, she writes the name of the friend who changed her life. Then she does it again on the next song, and the next.
For weeks, this path has followed the Masnavi, Rumi's long book of stories. But that isn't the whole of him. He also poured out short poems, a whole ocean of them, sung and recited among his friends.
And at the end of many, the name you'd expect to find is missing. Someone else's is there.

teach.b: Ghazal is an old Arabic word that became a Persian form: the short love poem. It's built from a run of couplets.

Every couplet ends on the same rhyme, and often the same repeated word or phrase, so the poem keeps circling back to one sound like a chorus. Each couplet can almost stand alone, a small bead on a string.

teach.h: THE LAST ONE CARRIES A NAME.
teach.b: By custom, the last couplet carries the poet's signature, a pen name tucked into the lines. Rumi wrote a great many of these; tradition counts them in the thousands.
They're gathered, along with many short quatrains, in a huge collection called the Divan-e Shams, the collected poems of Shams. And here's the surprise.
Remember Shams of Tabriz, the wandering dervish who arrived in Konya, turned Rumi's life over, and then vanished?
In the signature couplet, Rumi very often names Shams instead of himself, as if Shams were the poem's author, or its source. Sometimes he signs with a different word: khamush, Persian for silent.
A poem that ends by telling itself to hush.
Why sign with a friend's name? Honestly, only the poems survive, not his explanation. One reading: a lover losing himself in the beloved.
Shams is where the song came from, so Shams gets the name. The Masnavi, tradition says, was dictated to a student and read back, a teacher's book.
The ghazals are hotter and faster, often said to have come in the middle of music and turning. Same man, a different fire.

how: Rumi's ghazals are still recited and sung in Persian, often set to music, and Mevlevi gatherings use his poems in their ceremonies.

o: a short love poem of rhyming couplets, signed at the end
a list of rules for living, written in prose

games.q: you're Rumi. you've just finished a poem, and it's time for the signature couplet. whose name goes in?
o: Shams, the friend who set you on fire.
games.why: in many ghazals Rumi names Shams of Tabriz, as if Shams were the source of the poem. in others he signs with khamush, silent.

practice: Read one poem aloud, quietly and slowly, letting each line land: Rumi, or any poem you love, or a few lines you know by heart. If nothing comes, repeat one line you remember and listen to your own voice circling back.
The ghazal was made for the ear, not the page.
